domains.title: Love, Beauty, the Morning and Evening Star
domains.subtitle: The Mother of Aeneas, Namesake of the Planet
domains.lead: Venus is the Roman goddess of love and beauty — early and completely identified with Greek Aphrodite, but with a Roman political career the Greek original never had: mother of Aeneas, ancestress of the Romans, divine patron of the Julian line, and the planet’s namesake. From Lucretius’ opening hymn to the courtesan-cults of the seaports, she is Rome’s most versatile goddess — and the only one in this lexicon whose name needs no restoration at all.

cards.name: The Morning Star
cards.desc: The planet Venus — Lucifer at dawn, Vesper at dusk — is her celestial body, brightest in the sky.

cards.name: Mother of Aeneas
cards.desc: By the Trojan Anchises she bore Aeneas — and through him, the whole Roman race claimed her blood.

cards.name: Venus Genetrix
cards.desc: “Venus the Mother”: Caesar dedicated her a temple in the Forum of Caesar, claiming her line.

cards.name: The Foam-Born
cards.desc: The Greek myth made her sea-born of foam — the Roman poets kept the story and Latinized the name.

mythology.lead: Venus’ mythology is Aphrodite’s retold in a Roman accent — the foam-birth, the Judgement of Paris, the loves and the intrigues — plus a Roman coda the Greeks never wrote: the divine ancestress of Rome. Virgil’s Aeneid makes her the poem’s moving force, the goddess who shields her son through Troy’s fall to Italy’s shore; and the Julian gens made her their household god.

myths.title: The Foam-Birth
myths.text: The Greek story: Cronus’ severed genitals fell into the sea, and from the foam (aphros) rose the goddess, first at Cyprus’ shore. Roman poets from Ennius onward retold it with Venus’ name — the sea-foam’s child Latinized without effort, the island of Cyprus keeping the cult’s oldest address.

myths.title: The Judgement of Paris
myths.text: At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the uninvited Strife threw the golden apple ‘to the fairest’ — and Hera, Athena, and Venus asked the shepherd Paris to judge. Venus’ bribe, Helen, won; the judgement’s price was Troy. The Roman telling keeps every detail — only the goddess’ name has changed, and the empire’s stake in the story.

myths.title: The Mother of the Race
myths.text: Virgil gives Venus her Roman apotheosis: she saves Aeneas from Troy’s burning, guides him through the sea-wanderings to Italy, and by the divine machinery’s decree founds the line — ‘I am Caesar and his whole Julian race’ — that will rule the world. No Greek goddess had such a son; the epic made her Rome’s mother.

myths.title: The Onrushing of Creation
myths.text: The De Rerum Natura opens with the great hymn: ‘Venus, mother of Aeneas and his race, delight of men and gods, under your onrushing the leaping clouds flee’. Lucretius made her the Epicurean nature-principle — the generative urge that moves atoms and seasons — philosophy’s most surprising use of a love-goddess.

lore.syncretism: Venus absorbed Aphrodite wholesale — the earliest and most complete of the Greco-Roman identifications — and then Isis of the ports, the Syrian goddess of the sailors, and every eastern Astarte the legions met. The planet’s name passed through her to every European language; and the Christian polemics against ‘venereal’ error gave her name its modern shadow.
lore.culturalLegacy: The planet Venus is hers in every tongue that names the sky; the calendar’s Friday (veneris dies) still pays her; and ‘venereal’ keeps her name in the medical vocabulary. The Renaissance adored her — Botticelli’s Birth is her most reproduced image — and the word ‘Venus’ became, in plain Latin letters, the one goddess-name that never needed restoring.
lore.extendedMeditation: Venus: the only entry in the batch whose restoration is a tautology — the name has crossed every border unaltered for three thousand years. She stands in the lexicon as the control-group of the whole project: some names need diacritics to keep what ASCII loses; this one kept everything in plain letters from the start.

sources.name: Julius Caesar, Forum of Caesar dedication

lore.archaeology: The Forum of Caesar’s temple of Venus Genetrix, the House of the Vettii’s great fresco, the Venus de Milo and the Capitoline Venus — her monuments span the empire. The planet’s telescopic mapping keeps her name on the morning sky.
lore.cult: The Veneralia of April 1, the rites of Venus Erycina on the Capitol, and the courtesans’ cults of the seaports — hers was a religion of the body politic. The Julian line’s household worship made her the state’s ancestress.
lore.iconography: The sea-born goddess wringing her hair, the doves and the swan at her feet, the apple of the judgement in her hand; or the modest Capitoline type. Her icon is the beauty that starts wars — the smile that launched the ships.
lore.reception: Western art made her its favorite subject from Pompeii to the Salon; the word ‘Venus’ became the learned and then the common name for ideal beauty; and the planet’s brutal surface, mapped by her name, is astronomy’s favorite irony — the love-goddess’ world is the hottest hell in the sky.
